text: Last lesson introduced the lock manager in general terms. Now the first specific kind of lock: the shared lock, the one an ordinary read takes.

A plain SELECT, under the default READ COMMITTED isolation level, takes a shared, or S, lock on the rows it reads. Shared locks are compatible with other shared locks, so any number of sessions can hold one on the exact same row at the exact same time — reading doesn't change anything, so there's nothing for two readers to corrupt.

A shared lock is still a real lock, though. It is not compatible with an exclusive lock, the kind a write takes. That's exactly why, back in Lesson 102, Session B's SELECT had to wait on Session A's open UPDATE — shared and exclusive always conflict. The rule: shared locks conflict with writers, never with other readers.

Here's the detail that matters most going forward: under READ COMMITTED, a shared lock isn't held for the whole transaction. It's released the instant the read of that row finishes, even if the transaction around it is still open. An exclusive lock, by contrast, is held all the way to commit or rollback.

You can see this directly. Querying sys.dm_tran_locks while a transaction is mid-flight shows every granted and waiting lock, and the request_mode column reads S for a shared lock. You'll get the full walkthrough of this view in Lesson 110.

That early release is also exactly what opens the door to a nonrepeatable read later in this chapter — nothing stops another transaction from changing that row before yours commits. Next up: exclusive locks, the kind that actually holds on.
